description_full: Fidelity National Information Services, Inc. provides solutions to financial institutions, businesses, and developers worldwide. The company operates through Banking Solutions, Capital Market Solutions, and Corporate and Other segments. It provides core processing and ancillary applications; mobile and online banking; fraud, risk management, and compliance; card and retail payment; electronic funds transfer and network; wealth and retirement; and item processing and output solutions. The company also offers trading and assets, lending, leveraged and syndicated loan markets, and treasury and risk solutions. Fidelity National Information Services, Inc. was founded in 1968 and is headquartered in Jacksonville, Florida.

Each employee generates $56K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $4K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 17× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (10/10).
financial_summary: Fidelity National Information S is a large-cap technology business with a $15.2B market cap on $10.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -10% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 3% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 33%.

The business throws off $2.5B in free cash flow — roughly 23 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 6.83× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.4× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.5×.

Management returns a meaningful 14.9% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 16% operating margin runs 10pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 45% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 57% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 42% and a beta of 0.95, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.07 vs 5y 0.93), so read it loosely.

val: The stock trades 76% below its DCF fair value of $124, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 46%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $93.21 to $171 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 4.4 vs 27.4, EV/EBITDA 9.4 vs 17.1 and P/FCF 6.2 vs 26.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 69% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 16.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 22 covering analysts target $35.55 on average, 20% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 3% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 3.39).
It runs a 33% gross margin and converts 23% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 3% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.4x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 16pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 1.7% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.4x net debt to EBITDA ($599.0M of cash against $13.1B of debt), with interest covered 4.5x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of -0.10 in the distress zone.
The current ratio of 0.59 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
Goodwill makes up 53% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -9.8% over 3 years, -3.2% over 5 years and 4.9% over 10 years, so the decline is deepening, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 17%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -10.1% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 2.2x annual revenue and deferred revenue up 10%.
Capex runs only 0.1x depreciation (1.4% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 18, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only bought over the past year (5 purchases, net $1.2M bought).
It returns 14.9% a year to shareholders (9.4% in buybacks and 6.0% in dividends).

people: With about 44,000 employees, each generates about $243K of revenue, 0.7x the Technology median, and revenue has grown 6.7% a year across its filed history.
